h2: Eddy current testing in Dallas–Fort Worth: which assets get it and how to choose a supplier
html:
Eddy current testing in Dallas–Fort Worth: which assets get it and how to choose a supplier

Eddy current testing in Dallas–Fort Worth is used mostly on aircraft structure, on heat-exchanger and chiller tubing, and on conductive parts that need a fast surface-crack check without stripping paint. Atlantis sends ET technicians from Houston to sites across North Texas, works to a written procedure reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III, and quotes each scope once tube material, access and the governing code are known.

Airframes and rotorcraft. Fort Worth carries most of the region's aerospace work. Lockheed Martin builds the F-35 at Air Force Plant 4, and Bell Textron, headquartered in Fort Worth, runs six manufacturing facilities around the Metroplex, including the Manufacturing Technology Center where the V-280 Valor and 360 Invictus were developed. On this kind of hardware ET means bolt-hole and fastener-row inspection, cracks at radii and edges, and conductivity checks that confirm the temper of aluminum parts after heat treatment or heat damage. Production aerospace work requires NAS 410 personnel certification; Atlantis offers NAS 410 Level 3 support only through an associate.

Airline maintenance. Southwest Airlines is headquartered in Dallas and keeps a multi-hangar maintenance base at Love Field for its Boeing 737 fleet, while American Airlines Group is headquartered in Fort Worth. In airline work the eddy current technique, frequency and reference standard come from the manufacturer's NDT manual and the carrier's FAA-approved maintenance program, so the inspector follows the task card rather than choosing a method on the day.

Power plants and buildings. North Texas generation includes Comanche Peak near Glen Rose, about 40 miles southwest of Fort Worth: two Westinghouse four-loop pressurized water reactors operated by Irving-based Vistra under NRC Region IV oversight and licensed to 2050 and 2053. Steam generator tube examination at a nuclear unit is a specialist program of its own. The more common commercial jobs are condenser, feedwater heater and lube-oil cooler bundles at gas-fired and industrial plants, and the water-cooled chillers in office towers, hospitals and campus central plants, where bobbin-probe ET of copper tubes finds pitting, support-plate wear and freeze damage before a tube leaks.

People searching for eddy current testing companies or ECT inspection services usually have a bundle or a part and a fixed outage date. These questions separate suppliers quickly:

  • Tube material: copper alloy, stainless and titanium tubes suit conventional bobbin ECT; carbon steel tubes need remote field testing, near-field testing or IRIS.
  • Reference standard: the calibration tube should match the material, diameter and wall of the tubes being tested, with the artificial flaws ASME Section V Article 8 calls for.
  • Cleaning and fill factor: bundles must be cleaned, usually by hydroblasting, so a probe of the right diameter will pass.
  • Analysis and data: who reads the signals, and whether you receive the raw data and a tube map, not only a summary sheet.
  • Personnel: certification to the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice, or NAS 410 for aerospace.

The method and its limits are explained on the eddy current testing page, and ferrous tubing that needs ultrasonic wall measurement is covered on the IRIS tube inspection page. For a complete outage scope that combines ET with UT, PT or visual work, start from NDT inspection services. Technicians who want to qualify in the method can take eddy current testing training and practice signal interpretation on the Practical NDT eddy current simulator. To scope a North Texas job, send the tube count, material, sizes and outage window through the Dallas–Fort Worth ET request.
